title: Joshua 15:13–19
context: Within Judah's territory, Caleb receives Hebron as Moses and the LORD had promised, drives out the descendants of Anak, and offers his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever captures Kiriath Sepher (Debir). Othniel takes the city, and Achsah boldly asks her father for springs of water to make her southern land fruitful. A parallel account appears in Judges 1:10–15.

verses.text: He gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh a portion among the children of Judah, according to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua, even Kiriath Arba, named after the father of Anak (also called Hebron).
verses.arminianNotes: Caleb's portion fulfills Numbers 14:24, where God says Caleb "has followed me fully." Arminian readers stress the link between Caleb's wholehearted faith and the reward promised to him, as Joshua 14:14 also states.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase "according to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua." Caleb's inheritance rests on God's word, and his wholehearted following is itself a fruit of the "another spirit" God noted in him (Numbers 14:24).

verses.text: Caleb drove out the three sons of Anak: Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak.
verses.arminianNotes: Caleb drives out Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the very giants who frightened the spies (Numbers 13:22, 28). Arminian readers see faith that once stood against the crowd now acting in obedience and seeing God's word proven.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Judges 1:10 credits this victory to Judah more broadly. Caleb's personal triumph is part of God giving victory to his people, the strength of the giants being no obstacle to God's promise.

verses.text: He went up against the inhabitants of Debir: now the name of Debir before was Kiriath Sepher.
verses.arminianNotes: Debir was earlier struck by Joshua (Joshua 10:38–39), yet here it must be taken again. Arminian readers see that God's victories still call for continued faithful effort; possession is not automatic.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the repeated capture, often explained as the town being reoccupied after Joshua's campaign. Either way, God's gift unfolds in stages, and each stage is credited to his faithfulness.

verses.text: Caleb said, “He who strikes Kiriath Sepher, and takes it, to him I will give Achsah my daughter as wife.”
verses.arminianNotes: Caleb's offer of Achsah to the city's conqueror reflects ancient customs of marriage and reward. Arminian readers note that the story honors courage and initiative while not presenting the custom itself as a model for today.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the offer within its cultural setting and focus on the narrator's purpose: showing how faithful Caleb's household secures its inheritance. Descriptive details are not prescriptions.

verses.text: Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, took it: and he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife.
verses.arminianNotes: Othniel, "son of Kenaz," takes the city. Judges 1:13 calls him "Caleb's younger brother," though the Hebrew can be read as making Kenaz the brother. Arminian readers see a new generation sharing Caleb's faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Othniel later becomes the first judge, on whom "the LORD's Spirit came" (Judges 3:10). God is already preparing a deliverer within Caleb's faithful family before the crisis of Judges arrives.

verses.text: When she came, she had him ask her father for a field. She got off her donkey, and Caleb said, “What do you want?”
verses.arminianNotes: The Hebrew says Achsah urged Othniel to ask for a field; some ancient versions read it the other way. Either way, she speaks up herself in verse 19. Arminian readers admire her active, faith-filled initiative.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Achsah's request a picture of seeking good gifts from a generous father. God works through ordinary family conversations and practical requests to secure his people's flourishing in the land.

verses.text: She said, “Give me a blessing. Because you have set me in the land of the South, give me also springs of water.” So he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
verses.arminianNotes: "Give me a blessing" asks for springs to make dry southern land livable. Arminian readers see bold, persistent asking honored, a pattern of real requests that make a real difference in what is received.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Caleb gives more than asked, "the upper springs and the lower springs." Many see a reflection of the God who gives generously to his children; asking is the means God uses, and the giving rests on his goodness.
